messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 26
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 72

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Relaxation: avoid relaxing because it feels dangerous, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
  Memory: Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Ethan Reyes had been with the police department for six years and had built his reputation as a calm, observant detective, the kind of man other officers trusted to walk into ugly situations without flinching. Outside work he lived in a quiet apartment with his wife, Marisol, in a North American suburb where the routines were ordinary enough to make what happened to him feel even more disorienting in hindsight. The violence had come not from a stranger on the street but from a romantic partner he had once trusted completely. During the last months of that relationship, an argument in their apartment escalated into him being shoved against a counter, held down, and struck hard enough to leave him with bruises and cuts; he could still picture the kitchen light, the cramped hallway, and the smell of stale alcohol on the other person’s breath as the fear turned physical. He had escaped, but he never felt that the danger ended with the door closing behind him.

Even now, certain moments would pull him straight back. If he felt nauseous after a long shift or after missing a meal, the sensation could open the door to a memory that arrived against his will, vivid and painfully detailed. He would suddenly know again the exact angle of the room, the pressure of a hand on his shoulder, the sound of slurred words, and sometimes he felt as if the voices from that night were playing inside his head with the same harsh clarity. The smell of alcohol was even worse; catching it on a suspect’s breath, in a bar hallway, or on a bottle at home would bring the whole scene flooding in before he had time to steady himself. Seeing visible injuries on others had the same effect, especially fresh wounds or bruising during an arrest or at a scene, because they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe about people: that they could become cruel without warning, that people were not what they seemed. Each of those moments also reinforced a deeper conclusion. Ethan had lost his faith in people, life, and any higher power he might once have believed was keeping order in the world, and he had begun to see himself as permanently outside everyone else’s easy trust, as if what had happened had marked him in a way that could not be undone.

The more those memories came, the more he tried to shut down anything that might let them in. He stopped relaxing after work because stillness felt dangerous to him; if he let himself sit on the couch too long, his mind would wander and the memory would force its way in. He learned to numb his feelings by staying busy, working late, reviewing case files, taking on extra tasks, anything that kept him from noticing the fear underneath. Physical contact became unbearable in a way he could not explain cleanly to Marisol at first. He avoided being touched even in ordinary moments, flinching from a hand on his back or tensing when she reached for him in bed, because contact felt too close to the old helplessness and made him fear he would not be able to control what surfaced next. Those efforts helped him get through the day, but they also kept him on guard in a body that never seemed to settle. He was always scanning for injuries on suspects, for the sour trace of alcohol, for the uneasy feeling of nausea that might signal another intrusive surge. The more he tried to outrun the memories, the more trapped he felt in a life organized around not being caught off balance.

Over time, the habits that were supposed to protect him began to deepen the very convictions he feared. Because he kept his emotions locked down and withdrew from touch, he felt increasingly separate from other people, as if connection belonged to everyone else and not to him. Avoiding relaxation left him alone with his thoughts at odd hours, and the quiet made him dwell on the idea that no one was fully safe to trust. Even at home he had trouble letting Marisol see how frightened he was, and the distance between them made his belief that he was an outsider feel more real. He hated what this had done to him, but he also could not shake the sense that the world had shown its true face and that it was only sensible to stay guarded. That guardedness did not keep the past away, however. In the field, the sights and smells he encountered kept setting off memories, and every time the images and voices returned he tightened his control even further. He became more vigilant with anything that resembled the original event, and ordinary life narrowed around his efforts to avoid being pulled under again.

By the time he came in for help, it was because the pattern was starting to cost him the parts of life he still cared about. He had noticed himself pulling away from Marisol, shrinking from her touch, and he was afraid she would eventually stop trying. He worried too that his work, which had once been the one place he could trust his competence, was becoming harder to manage because the same injuries and alcohol smells that turned up in his cases kept breaking open the memories. Ethan was not looking for a neat explanation so much as relief from the constant alertness and the sense that he had become cut off from ordinary human closeness. What he most feared was that the world really was as dangerous and false as it now seemed, and what he most hoped was that he might learn how to stay present with his wife and his life without every nausea, bruise, or whiff of alcohol dragging him back into that room.
